subject: Biology
title: Tropical Rainforests
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Tropical Rainforests.

hook.text: Tropical rainforests cover just 6% of Earth's land but hold more than half of all species.

buildup.text: Warm temperatures and heavy rainfall year-round create layers of life from floor to canopy.

discovery.text: The canopy is so thick that only 2% of sunlight reaches the forest floor.

twist.text: Rainforest soil is surprisingly poor. Most nutrients are locked in living plants, not the ground.

climax.text: Deforestation destroys these fragile systems. Once cleared, rainforest soil becomes barren fast.

punchline.text: The richest forests grow on the poorest soil.

quiz.question: Why is rainforest soil surprisingly poor?
options: Most nutrients are in living plants, not soil

details.summary: Tropical rainforests receive over 2,000 millimeters of rainfall annually and harbor more than half of all terrestrial species on just 6 percent of land. Their layered canopy structure creates diverse microhabitats from forest floor to emergent treetops reaching 60 meters high.
details.whyItMatters: Rainforests regulate global climate by absorbing CO2 and recycling water. They contain millions of undiscovered species and potential medicines. Deforestation threatens these irreplaceable ecosystems and accelerates climate change.
takeaways: Tropical rainforests contain over half of all terrestrial species
The canopy structure creates distinct vertical layers with unique communities
Rainforests generate their own rainfall through evapotranspiration

faq.question: Why are tropical rainforests so biodiverse?
faq.answer: Consistent warmth and abundant rainfall support year-round growth. Stable climate over millions of years allowed species accumulation. Complex vertical structure from floor to canopy creates many niches. High productivity provides abundant energy to support diverse life.

faq.question: How do tropical rainforests affect global climate?
faq.answer: They absorb and store billions of tons of carbon. Through evapotranspiration, they generate rainfall not just locally but for regions thousands of kilometers away. The Amazon alone produces about 20 percent of the oxygen entering Earth's atmosphere.
